stem: A student records the time taken for a reaction in a results table. Which column is set out correctly?

options.content: Heading: **time**; entries such as 45 s
options.rationale: The unit belongs in the heading, not in every cell.

options.content: Heading: **time / s**; entries such as 45
options.rationale: Quantity and unit in the heading; numbers only in the body.

options.content: Heading: **seconds**; entries such as 45
options.rationale: The heading should name the quantity (time) as well as the unit.

options.content: Heading: **time / s**; entries such as 45 s
options.rationale: Once the unit is in the heading it is not repeated in the cells.

explanation: Each column heading gives the quantity and its unit (time / s), and the cells contain only numbers.

stem: Match each set of data with the most suitable type of graph.

left.content: The rate of an enzyme reaction measured at 10, 20, 30, 40 and 50 °C
The mean mass of protein in 100 g of beans, kapenta, maize meal and milk
The number of leaves in each length class: 20–29 mm, 30–39 mm, 40–49 mm and 50–59 mm

explanation: Temperature and rate are both continuous, so a line graph is used. The foods are separate categories, so a bar chart (with gaps) is used. Leaf lengths are continuous data grouped into classes with a frequency for each, so a histogram (bars touching) is used.
hints: Ask: is the independent variable a number on a scale, a category, or a class of values?

stem: True or false: on a line graph, the independent variable is normally plotted on the x-axis.

answerSpec.feedbackTrue: Correct: the independent variable goes on the x-axis (horizontal) and the dependent variable on the y-axis.
answerSpec.feedbackFalse: It is true. The variable you changed goes on the x-axis; the one you measured goes on the y-axis.

explanation: By convention the independent variable (the one changed) is plotted on the x-axis and the dependent variable (the one measured) on the y-axis.

stem: A potato cylinder has a mass of 3.20 g. After 40 minutes in distilled water its mass is 3.68 g. Calculate the percentage change in mass.
explanation: The mass increased by $3.68 - 3.20 = 0.48$ g. Percentage change $= \frac{0.48}{3.20} \times 100 = 15.0\%$.
workedSolution:
1. Change in mass $= 3.68 - 3.20 = 0.48\ \text{g}$ (an increase).
2. Percentage change $= \frac{0.48}{3.20} \times 100$.
3. $= 15.0\%$.
hints: Divide the change by the starting mass, not the final mass.

stem: A piece of sweet potato had a mass of 4.50 g before it was placed in a concentrated salt solution, and 3.96 g afterwards. Calculate the percentage change in mass. Show a decrease as a negative value.
explanation: The mass fell by $4.50 - 3.96 = 0.54$ g. Percentage change $= \frac{-0.54}{4.50} \times 100 = -12.0\%$.
workedSolution:
1. Change in mass $= 3.96 - 4.50 = -0.54\ \text{g}$ (a decrease).
2. Percentage change $= \frac{-0.54}{4.50} \times 100 = -12.0\%$.
3. Dividing by the final mass instead ($\frac{0.54}{3.96}$) would wrongly give 13.6%.
hints: Subtract the starting mass from the final mass: the answer is negative for a loss.

stem: Four repeat readings of the time taken for a colour change were 58 s, 61 s, 96 s and 60 s. Calculate the mean time, leaving out the anomalous result. Give your answer to the nearest second.
explanation: 96 s is anomalous (far from the other readings). Mean $= \frac{58 + 61 + 60}{3} = \frac{179}{3} = 59.7$ s, which is 60 s to the nearest second.
workedSolution:
1. Identify the anomaly: 96 s is much longer than the other three readings.
2. Mean of the rest $= \frac{58 + 61 + 60}{3} = \frac{179}{3} = 59.67\ \text{s}$.
3. To the nearest second: $60\ \text{s}$.
hints: Which reading does not fit the pattern?

stem: In an enzyme investigation, the starch in one tube took 140 s to disappear. Calculate the rate of reaction as $\frac{1000}{\text{time}}$. Give your answer to 2 decimal places.
explanation: Rate $= \frac{1000}{140} = 7.142857\ldots = 7.14$ to 2 decimal places.
hints: Divide 1000 by the time in seconds.

stem: Chipo planted 25 groundnut seeds. After a week, 17 had germinated. What percentage of the seeds germinated?
explanation: Percentage germinated $= \frac{17}{25} \times 100 = 68\%$.

stem:
A student measured the height of froth produced when liver was added to hydrogen peroxide at different temperatures.

| Temperature / °C | Height of froth / mm, test 1 | test 2 | test 3 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 20 | 18 | 20 | 19 |
| 30 | 31 | 29 | 30 |
| 40 | 42 | 25 | 44 |
| 50 | 12 | 14 | 13 |

Which result is anomalous?

options.content: 18 mm at 20 °C
options.rationale: This is close to the other readings at 20 °C.

options.content: 31 mm at 30 °C
options.rationale: This is close to the other readings at 30 °C.

options.content: 25 mm at 40 °C
options.rationale: The other two readings at 40 °C are 42 mm and 44 mm.

options.content: 12 mm at 50 °C
options.rationale: All three readings at 50 °C are low, so they fit together; the enzyme is being denatured.

explanation: An anomalous result does not fit the pattern of the repeats. At 40 °C, 42 mm and 44 mm agree closely, but 25 mm does not. The low readings at 50 °C agree with each other, so they are a real effect, not an anomaly.
hints: Compare each reading with the other repeats at the same temperature.

stem: What should a student do with an anomalous result when calculating a mean?

options.content: Include it, because every result must be used.
options.rationale: An anomaly would make the mean misleading.

options.content: Change it to a value that fits the pattern.
options.rationale: Changing data is never acceptable.

options.content: Delete all the results and start again.
options.rationale: The other results are still useful.

options.content: Leave it out of the mean and, if possible, repeat that test.
options.rationale: The mean is then based only on results that fit together.

explanation: An anomalous result is left out of the mean (and marked, for example by circling it), and the test is repeated if there is time. Results must never be altered.

stem:
The table shows the mean height of some bean seedlings.

| Time / days | 0 | 2 | 4 | 6 | 8 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Mean height / mm | 0 | 6 | 14 | 24 | 36 |

The points are plotted and joined with ruled straight lines. Use the graph to estimate the mean height on day 7.
explanation: Day 7 is halfway between day 6 (24 mm) and day 8 (36 mm). On a straight line joining these points, the height is halfway between them: $\frac{24 + 36}{2} = 30$ mm.
workedSolution:
1. Find the points either side of day 7: day 6 (24 mm) and day 8 (36 mm).
2. Day 7 is halfway between them, so read halfway up the line: $24 + \frac{36 - 24}{2} = 30\ \text{mm}$.
hints: Day 7 lies exactly halfway between two of the plotted points.

stem: The time for starch to disappear when amylase was added was 480 s at 10 °C, 220 s at 20 °C, 110 s at 30 °C and 60 s at 40 °C. Which is the best conclusion?

options.content: As the temperature increased from 10 °C to 40 °C, the time decreased from 480 s to 60 s, so amylase worked faster at higher temperatures in this range.
options.rationale: It describes the trend, quotes data and does not go beyond the range tested.

options.content: Amylase works best at 40 °C.
options.rationale: No temperatures above 40 °C were tested, so the optimum could be higher.

options.content: The time changed when the temperature changed.
options.rationale: Too vague: it does not say how it changed or quote any data.

options.content: All enzymes are fastest at 40 °C.
options.rationale: Only one enzyme was tested; this claims far more than the data show.

explanation: A good conclusion describes the trend, uses values from the data, and stays within what was tested. Because 40 °C was the highest temperature used, the data cannot show the optimum.
hints: Which statement quotes the data and does not claim more than was tested?

stem: In an amylase experiment, students found it hard to decide exactly when a drop of the mixture stopped turning iodine solution blue-black. Which improvement deals with this problem?

options.content: Use more iodine solution in each spot.
options.rationale: This does not make the end-point any easier to judge.

options.content: Test the mixture less often.
options.rationale: This makes the timing less precise.

options.content: Compare each spot with a colour standard of iodine solution mixed with water.
options.rationale: A standard shows exactly what 'no starch' looks like, so the end-point is judged the same way each time.

options.content: Use a larger beaker as the water bath.
options.rationale: This does not affect how the colour is judged.

explanation: The source of error is judging a colour change by eye. Comparing with a colour standard (iodine with no starch) or using a colorimeter makes the end-point consistent.
hints: The problem is judging a colour by eye: what would give a fixed comparison?

stem: True or false: in a results table, the unit should be written after every number in the column.

answerSpec.feedbackTrue: Not true. The unit goes once, in the column heading (for example mass / g); the cells contain only numbers.
answerSpec.feedbackFalse: Correct. The unit appears once in the heading, such as time / s.

explanation: Units are written in the column heading after the quantity (for example temperature / °C). The body of the table contains only numbers.

stem: A student weighs some leaves on a balance that reads to 0.01 g.

payload.template: Each mass should be recorded to {{blank:dp}} decimal places, so a mass of exactly three grams is recorded in the table as {{blank:mass}}.

explanation: A balance that reads to 0.01 g gives two decimal places, so every mass is recorded to 2 decimal places: 3.00, not 3 or 3.0.
hints: How many decimal places does a reading such as 0.01 g have?

stem: Which of these is good practice in a biological drawing?

options.content: Shade the drawing to show which parts are darker.
options.rationale: Shading hides detail: use clear outlines only.

options.content: Use clear, continuous lines and no shading.
options.rationale: This shows the outlines of the structures clearly.

options.content: Draw label lines with arrowheads that cross each other.
options.rationale: Label lines are ruled, do not cross and have no arrowheads.

options.content: Make the drawing small so that it fits in a corner.
options.rationale: Drawings should be large, filling most of the space provided.

explanation: Biological drawings use a sharp pencil, clear continuous lines, no shading, correct proportions and ruled label lines that touch the structure and do not cross.

stem:
Two students each measured the length of the same leaf three times. The true length is 52 mm.

| Student | Reading 1 / mm | Reading 2 / mm | Reading 3 / mm |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Rudo | 46 | 46 | 47 |
| Sipho | 50 | 55 | 51 |

Which statement is correct?

options.content: Rudo's results are more reliable, but Sipho's mean is closer to the true value.
options.rationale: Rudo's readings agree closely; Sipho's mean (52 mm) equals the true length.

options.content: Rudo's results are both reliable and accurate.
options.rationale: They agree closely (reliable) but are about 6 mm below the true value, so they are not accurate.

options.content: Sipho's results are more reliable than Rudo's.
options.rationale: Sipho's readings vary by 5 mm; Rudo's agree to within 1 mm.

options.content: Neither set of results can be used because they differ.
options.rationale: Both sets can be evaluated; differences tell us about reliability and accuracy.

explanation: Reliability is about how closely repeat readings agree: Rudo's (46, 46, 47) agree better than Sipho's (50, 55, 51). Accuracy is closeness to the true value: Sipho's mean is $\frac{50 + 55 + 51}{3} = 52$ mm, exactly the true length, while Rudo's mean (46.3 mm) is too low, perhaps because she measured from the end of the ruler instead of from zero.
hints: Work out each student's mean and compare it with 52 mm.
Reliable means the repeats agree; accurate means close to the true value.

stem:
Rudo investigated the effect of temperature on the digestion of starch by amylase. She recorded the time taken for the starch to disappear.

| Temperature / °C | Time 1 / s | Time 2 / s | Time 3 / s | Mean time / s |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 10 | 420 | 435 | 410 | 422 |
| 20 | 240 | 228 | 236 | 235 |
| 30 | 130 | 124 | 190 | |
| 40 | 75 | 80 | 76 | 77 |
| 50 | 160 | 152 | 158 | 157 |

options.content: 410 s at 10 °C
options.rationale: It is close to the other readings at 10 °C.

options.content: 240 s at 20 °C
options.rationale: It is close to the other readings at 20 °C.

options.content: 190 s at 30 °C
options.rationale: The other readings at 30 °C are 130 s and 124 s.

options.content: 160 s at 50 °C
options.rationale: All three readings at 50 °C are similar.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Calculate the mean time at 30 °C, leaving out the anomalous result.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Calculate the rate of reaction at 30 °C as $\frac{1000}{\text{mean time}}$. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Describe the effect of temperature on the time taken for the starch to disappear. Use data from the table.

points.description: From 10 °C to 40 °C the time decreases (from 422 s to 77 s)
Shortest time / fastest at 40 °C; above 40 °C (at 50 °C) the time increases again (to 157 s)

parts.explanation: As the temperature rose from 10 °C to 40 °C, the mean time fell from 422 s to 77 s. The time was shortest at 40 °C. At 50 °C the time increased again, to 157 s.

parts.label: (e)
parts.stem: Suggest **one** improvement that would help Rudo find the optimum temperature more precisely.

points.description: Test more temperatures between 30 °C and 50 °C, e.g. 35, 40, 45 °C (smaller intervals around the peak)

parts.explanation: Test extra temperatures close to the peak, for example 35 °C and 45 °C, because the optimum could lie anywhere between 30 °C and 50 °C.

explanation: 190 s at 30 °C is anomalous. The mean of 130 s and 124 s is 127 s, and the rate is $\frac{1000}{127} = 7.9$. The time is shortest at 40 °C and rises at 50 °C, so the optimum lies somewhere between 30 °C and 50 °C.
workedSolution:
1. (a) 190 s does not fit with 130 s and 124 s.
2. (b) Mean $= \frac{130 + 124}{2} = 127\ \text{s}$ (including 190 s would give a wrong mean of 148 s).
3. (c) Rate $= \frac{1000}{127} = 7.874\ldots = 7.9$ to 1 decimal place.
4. (d) Time falls from 422 s at 10 °C to 77 s at 40 °C, then rises to 157 s at 50 °C.
5. (e) Add temperatures such as 35 °C and 45 °C.
hints: For (e), where could the optimum be?

stem:
Five students measured their pulse rates at rest and immediately after two minutes of skipping.

| Student | Resting pulse / beats per minute | Pulse after skipping / beats per minute |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A | 68 | 112 |
| B | 72 | 126 |
| C | 75 | 120 |
| D | 80 | 132 |
| E | 70 | 119 |

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Calculate the percentage increase in the pulse rate of student B.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Which type of graph is the most suitable for showing these results?

options.content: A line graph of pulse rate against student
options.rationale: The students are separate categories, so the points should not be joined.

options.content: A histogram of pulse rates
options.rationale: A histogram shows how many values fall into each class, which is not the aim here.

options.content: A pie chart for each student
options.rationale: Pie charts show proportions of a whole, not two separate measurements.

options.content: A bar chart with a pair of bars (rest and after skipping) for each student
options.rationale: The students are categories; paired bars allow easy comparison.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: The students counted beats for 30 seconds and doubled the number, instead of counting for 10 seconds and multiplying by 6. Explain why this is more accurate.

points.description: A miscount of one beat matters less over a longer count
Over 30 s a one-beat error gives an error of 2 beats per minute, but over 10 s it gives 6 beats per minute

parts.explanation: Counting for longer reduces the effect of a small counting error. If a student misses one beat, the error in the pulse rate is 1 × 2 = 2 beats per minute for a 30-second count, but 1 × 6 = 6 beats per minute for a 10-second count.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Suggest **one** reason why student D's results might not be comparable with the others.

points.description: D may have skipped faster / harder, or be less fit, or not have rested long enough before the resting reading

parts.explanation: Student D may have skipped faster than the others (the intensity of exercise was not controlled), or may not have been fully rested before the resting pulse was taken.

explanation: Student B's pulse rose by 126 − 72 = 54 beats per minute, an increase of $\frac{54}{72} \times 100 = 75\%$. The students are categories, so a bar chart is used. Longer counts reduce the effect of counting errors.
workedSolution:
1. (a) Increase $= 126 - 72 = 54$; percentage increase $= \frac{54}{72} \times 100 = 75\%$.
2. (b) Bar chart with paired bars.
3. (c) One missed beat: 2 bpm error (30 s count) versus 6 bpm error (10 s count).
4. (d) The intensity of exercise or the rest before the first reading may have differed.
hints: For (a), divide the increase by the resting value.

stem:
Tendai wants to estimate the number of black-jack plants in a rectangular part of the school field that measures 30 m by 20 m. He uses a square quadrat with sides of 50 cm. His counts in ten quadrats are:

4, 7, 3, 0, 6, 5, 8, 2, 5, 0

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Describe how Tendai should place the quadrats at random.

points.description: Mark out the area as a grid using two tape measures along the edges
Use random numbers (e.g. a random number generator or table) to choose coordinates, and place the quadrat at each

parts.explanation: He should lay two tape measures at right angles along two edges of the area to make a grid, then use a random number generator to choose pairs of coordinates and place the quadrat at each one.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Calculate the mean number of black-jack plants per quadrat.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Estimate the total number of black-jack plants in the area.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Explain why placing the quadrats where there seemed to be many plants would give an unreliable estimate.

points.description: The samples would be biased / not representative, so the estimate would be too high

parts.explanation: Choosing places with many plants biases the sample: it is not representative of the whole area, so the estimate would be too high.

explanation: Random sampling avoids bias. The mean is $\frac{40}{10} = 4$ plants per quadrat. Each quadrat has an area of $0.5 \times 0.5 = 0.25\ \text{m}^2$, so the density is $4 \div 0.25 = 16$ plants per m². The area is $30 \times 20 = 600\ \text{m}^2$, so the estimate is $16 \times 600 = 9600$ plants.
workedSolution:
1. (b) Total $= 4 + 7 + 3 + 0 + 6 + 5 + 8 + 2 + 5 + 0 = 40$; mean $= 40 \div 10 = 4$ per quadrat.
2. (c) Quadrat area $= 0.50 \times 0.50 = 0.25\ \text{m}^2$, so density $= 4 \div 0.25 = 16$ per m².
3. Area sampled $= 30 \times 20 = 600\ \text{m}^2$; estimate $= 16 \times 600 = 9600$ plants.
4. A common error is to treat the quadrat as 1 m², giving 2400.
hints: Convert the quadrat's side to metres before finding its area.
How many quadrats would fit into one square metre?

stem: Nyasha's drawing of a maize grain is 72 mm long. The actual grain is 12 mm long. Calculate the magnification of her drawing.
explanation: Magnification = length of drawing ÷ actual length $= \frac{72}{12} = \times 6$. Both lengths must be in the same units (here mm).
workedSolution:
1. Magnification $= \frac{\text{length of drawing}}{\text{actual length}}$.
2. $= \frac{72\ \text{mm}}{12\ \text{mm}} = 6$.
3. Magnification $= \times 6$ (no units).
hints: Divide the drawing length by the real length.

stem: A student plots a line graph. The dependent variable ranges from 0 to 42. The y-axis is 10 large squares tall. Which scale is the most suitable?

options.content: 1 unit per large square
options.rationale: Only values up to 10 would fit on the axis.

options.content: 5 units per large square
options.rationale: The axis reaches 50, so the data use more than half of it, and the scale is easy to read.

options.content: 7 units per large square
options.rationale: Awkward scales such as 7 make plotting and reading values difficult.

options.content: 20 units per large square
options.rationale: The data would use less than a quarter of the axis.

explanation: A good scale is easy to read (1, 2, 5 or 10 units per square, or multiples of 10 of these) and makes the plotted points use more than half the grid. With 5 units per large square the axis goes to 50, so values up to 42 fill most of it.
hints: Check that 42 fits, and that the points will use more than half the axis.

stem: True or false: the rate of an enzyme reaction can be calculated as 1 ÷ the time taken, so a shorter time gives a higher rate.

answerSpec.feedbackTrue: Correct. If the time halves, 1 ÷ time doubles.
answerSpec.feedbackFalse: It is true: rate = 1 ÷ time, so the shorter the time, the faster the rate.

explanation: When the time for a reaction to finish (or reach an end-point) is measured, rate = 1 ÷ time. A reaction that takes 50 s has twice the rate of one that takes 100 s.
